why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
claim: Two of this type's four filters are printed on one conversion column, and the unit returns one table through both of them. The column's fifteen frequencies are the third octaves from 250 Hz to 6.3 kHz with a sixteenth entry that is the filter switched out, and read on the generator's own low pass the corners land a median 0.018 octaves off the printed entry and never more than 0.065 -- 19 per cent of one step of the column, over 16 readings of its 15 entries. The disc generator's low pass, a different byte on the same column inside the same type, returns the same corners to a median 0.053 octaves, and 15 of 16 land inside what that sparser source failed to repeat at the corner being read. Both are one pole. Rendered onto the same band set and read by the same corner reader, a single pole falls -2.97 decibels an octave at its own corner and -5.60 past it, where a pair falls -5.86 and -11.94; the generator low pass measures -3.10 and -5.90, and the disc low pass -3.05 and -5.90. The eight-value quantum is readable from inside one run rather than assumed: settings 8 and 15 fall in one printed entry and return corners 0.0018 octaves apart, while setting 0 one entry below returns one 0.415 octaves away -- a ratio of 237. What the same run says about the third filter is a negative and a structural one. The type's own filter, at 40 03 05 on the neighbouring column, moved the generators' output by no more than 0.54 decibels at any of eighteen settings and across its own off switch, on takes repeating to 0.04 decibels and standing 52 decibels over the run's silence -- material the same reader pulled 49.5 decibels of filter out of one byte away. The noise generators are not behind that filter.
named: one sixteen-entry corner table, read by two one-pole sections
adds: The records say what each byte did to every twelfth-octave band at eighteen settings, with the band set, the control, the silence and the channel each was read from. What is read out of them here is where the corner sits, how fast the skirt runs at it and past it, that the two bytes return the same corners, that those corners are the frequencies the page prints, and that the third filter is not in the path at all. The records name no corner, no order and no table, and say so.
refutedBy: A third byte on this column returning corners that are not these -- the hum generator's low pass at 40 03 0F is printed on it and has not been read, and the reason it has not is that a hum is a line spectrum whose twelfth-octave profile is a reading of where its harmonics are rather than of a filter. A skirt anywhere on this column running at twelve decibels an octave would take the order with it. And a note played through this type with 40 03 05 swept, returning nothing, would take the structural half of this back: the claim is that the generators are summed after that filter, which requires it to be somewhere.
whatItWouldChange: A Lo-Fi 2 is three noise generators summed after the signal's own filter rather than through it, so a renderer that puts the generators inside the filter is wrong at every setting of a byte the page gives no path for.
Two of this part's corner tables are one pole, which prices an entry at one coefficient and holds the cost argument the frequency class rests on.

eraPriors.claim: A pole costs one stored coefficient and a conjugate pair costs two, so a sixteen-entry corner table spends sixteen numbers on one pole and thirty-two on a pair. A part that spends a filter on each of three noise generators is spending it where nobody will listen closely, which is where the cheap section goes if the part has one.
eraPriors.why: The frequency class was carried by the argument that sixteen entries are affordable and a hundred and twenty-eight are not, and what an entry holds is the quantity that argument is about. These two filters sit on the least audible thing in the type, so if any section in this part is the cheap one they are, and both came back on the cheap side.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: Either skirt ran at twelve decibels an octave. A pair measured on a noise generator's low pass would say the part pays for one where it least needs to, after which nothing about cost bounds what any of its other tables hold.

alternatives.reading: Two tables holding the same sixteen numbers rather than one table reached by two bytes.

separatedBy.observable: Nothing this rig can measure. Two tables holding identical entries and one table read twice return the same corner at every setting by construction, and a band profile is a reading of the corner.

predicts.one table: the same corner at every setting
predicts.two identical tables: the same corner at every setting

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: 0.053 octaves, which is what the two bytes already agree to.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: The two readings differ in nothing a measurement can reach. What the agreement does rule out is two tables holding different numbers, which is the thing worth ruling out: a filter given entries of its own has no reason to land within a sixth of a step of the other's at fifteen settings.

alternatives.reading: The corners are sixteen frequencies at equal ratios between the printed ends rather than the printed third octaves themselves.

separatedBy.observable: Where each entry sits, in octaves, on a range whose printed ends do not bracket a whole number of third octaves. This column's ends are 250 Hz and 6.3 kHz, which is exactly fifteen third octaves, so the two series are the same series here and no reading of this byte can tell them apart.

predicts.sixteen equal ratios: the same fifteen frequencies to within a third of a per cent

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: 0.018 octaves, the median this run put a corner off its printed entry.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: It is the same alternative the frequency class carries, and it is separated on a range whose ends are not a whole number of third octaves apart rather than here. This record adds a third range to the class and cannot close it.

alternatives.reading: The type's own filter is in the generators' path and its byte does nothing anywhere, rather than the generators being summed after it.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The same byte on the same printed column read on a type that has a signal in front of it. A chorus's and a flanger's pre-filter sit on column nine at 40 03 03 and 40 03 04, and both move a band profile by tens of decibels across the same settings. A byte that does nothing does nothing there too.
